item.text: {"text":"Temporal modeling offers a different hypothesis from stronger terminal supervision: learn which historical interactions matter across irregular time gaps. [TiSASRec](https://jiachengli1995.github.io/files/wsdm20.pdf) (2020) combines absolute positions with pairwise time intervals in self-attention; its temporal mechanism is relevant, although its backbone should not replace BERT4Rec. [TemProxRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09784) (2024) models temporal proximity through contrastive learning and self-attention with absolute and relative temporal/positional embeddings. [TiSRec](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3759327) (RecSys 2025) dynamically segments histories into local preference blocks using significant time intervals, then models preferences within and across blocks. These approaches motivate learning temporal relevance rather than treating sequence distance as elapsed time.\n\nStronger recency is not automatically beneficial: [Measuring Recency Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) (2024) reports that excessive emphasis on recent interactions harms performance in its experiments. A compatible experimental adaptation—not an established result from these papers—is to retain BERT4Rec’s bidirectional masked-item objective and add jointly learned, per-head attention-logit biases indexed by signed position distance and bucketed historical time differences. Unconstrained bias values can favor recent or older interactions without imposing monotonic decay. Use only observed history timestamps; give the appended prediction mask a dedicated unknown-time relation instead of using the held-out target timestamp. Preserve appended-mask inference and final-nonpadding readout. Compare position-only, time-only and combined biases under the fixed macro validation HR@10 protocol; the cited findings do not establish gains on these four Amazon categories."}
